Lord Canterville’s refusal troubled Mr. Otis considerably, and he begged him to change his mind. But the kindly nobleman stood firm and finally persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the ghost’s gift. In the spring of 1890, when the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented to the Queen at her first reception of the season, following the Duchess’s marriage, everyone admired her jewels. Virginia had received the ducal crown that rewards all good little American girls, marrying her young sweetheart as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming and so deeply in love that almost everyone welcomed the marriage. One exception was the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had hoped to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had hosted three expensive dinner parties to that end. Strangely, the other exception was Mr. Otis himself. He liked the young Duke very much personally, but objected to titles in principle. As he put it, he feared that “the weakening influence of an aristocracy devoted to pleasure might make people forget the true principles of republican simplicity.” His objections were completely overruled. I believe that when he walked his daughter up the aisle of St. George’s in Hanover Square, her hand on his arm, no man in England was prouder.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess visited Canterville Chase. The afternoon after they arrived, they walked to the lonely churchyard beside the pine woods. Choosing the inscription for Sir Simon’s gravestone had at first caused much difficulty. Eventually, they decided to carve only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess brought beautiful roses and scattered them over the grave. After standing beside it for a while, they walked into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. She sat on a fallen column while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing into her lovely eyes. Suddenly he tossed the cigarette away, took her hand, and said, “Virginia, a wife should keep no secrets from her husband.”

“Dear Cecil, I have no secrets from you.”

“Yes, you do,” he said with a smile. “You’ve never told me what happened when you were shut away with the ghost.”

“I have never told anyone, Cecil,” Virginia replied seriously.

“Basil, how extraordinary! I have to meet Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose and paced through the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is simply a source of artistic inspiration to me. You might see nothing special in him. I see everything. Sometimes he is most present in my work when it contains no picture of him at all. As I said, he suggests a new style. I find him in the curves of particular lines and in the beauty and delicate shades of certain colors. That is all.”

“Then why refuse to exhibit his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I put something of this strange artistic worship into it. Naturally, I have never wanted to tell him about that. He knows nothing, and he must never know. But other people might guess, and I refuse to expose my soul to their shallow, nosy eyes. I won’t let them examine my heart under a microscope. There is too much of me in that painting, Harry—far too much!”

“Poets have fewer principles than you. They know how useful passion is when you want to publish. These days, a broken heart can sell edition after edition.”

“And I hate them for it,” Hallward exclaimed. “Artists should make beautiful things without putting their own lives into them. Nowadays people treat art as though it should be autobiography. We have lost our feeling for beauty in itself. One day I will show the world what that means. For that very reason, the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you’re mistaken, Basil, but I won’t argue. Only people who have lost their intellectual way bother arguing. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter thought for a moment. “He likes me,” he said at last. “I know that much. Of course, I flatter him terribly. I get a strange pleasure from telling him things I know I will regret saying. Usually he is charming, and we sit in the studio discussing a thousand different subjects. Sometimes, though, he is dreadfully thoughtless and seems to enjoy hurting me. Then, Harry, I feel that I have given my entire soul to someone who treats it like a flower for his coat: a decoration to please his vanity, an ornament to wear on a summer day.”

“You haven’t been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy its evening gatherings.”

“Oh, no. The usual sort has nothing to offer me. I don’t play cards.”

“You didn’t before, I know. You never used to like cards, but time changes many things.”

“I haven’t changed that much yet,” Anne exclaimed. Then she stopped, afraid her words might be misunderstood, though she scarcely knew how. After a brief silence, he spoke as if moved by a sudden feeling. “It is a long time, certainly. Eight and a half years is a long time.”

Whether he would have said more was something Anne would have to wonder about later, when she was calmer. His words were still sounding in her ears when Henrietta abruptly drew her attention elsewhere. Eager to use this quiet moment to go out, Henrietta urged her companions to hurry before anyone else arrived.

They had to get moving. Anne said she was quite ready and tried to look it. But leaving that chair and preparing to leave the room filled her with regret and reluctance. If Henrietta had known what was in her heart, Anne felt, her own feelings for her cousin—and her certainty that he loved her—would have given her every reason to pity Anne.

Their preparations were suddenly interrupted. They heard alarming sounds as more visitors approached, and the door opened to admit Sir Walter and Miss Elliot. Their arrival seemed to chill everyone. Anne immediately felt weighed down, and wherever she looked she saw others affected in the same way. The room’s ease, freedom, and cheerfulness vanished. In response to the cold elegance of her father and sister, people became stiffly composed, deliberately silent, or busy with dull conversation. How humiliating to realize this!

Her watchful eye found comfort in one detail. Both acknowledged Captain Wentworth again, and Elizabeth did so more graciously than before. She even spoke to him once and looked at him several times. Elizabeth was, in fact, considering a significant step, as soon became clear. After wasting a few minutes on polite remarks of no importance, she began inviting everyone to an event intended to fulfill all her remaining obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends; nothing formal.” She spoke very gracefully. She laid her prepared cards, reading “Miss Elliot at home,” on the table, smiling politely at everyone. One card and one smile were directed especially toward Captain Wentworth. Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to appreciate the value of a man with his bearing and appearance.
